mappings.note: A median passes through the CENTROID, so the centroid is computed and substituted into the line. Centroid is the 2:1 section point of a median, hence LO-2.

Area of a triangle from its vertices - one of only a handful of area items in the whole chapter. Not LO-2, because nothing is being shown collinear. Stem is unusable as printed: the vertices exist only in a figure that does not travel with the question.
Perpendicular distance from the x-axis, the distance formula with a common abscissa.
Distance between two points that both sit on the y-axis, so the formula reduces to the difference of ordinates. Distance outcome.
Distance of a point from the origin by the distance formula.
Distance between a point on the y-axis and a point on the x-axis - both coordinates change, so the full formula is needed.
Diagonal of a rectangle given three vertices: identify the diagonal, then apply the distance formula. No area and no section formula.
Perimeter is the three side lengths added, so the distance formula three times. Area is NOT asked, so C-4.2-LO-1 is out.
A perpendicular bisector must pass through the MIDPOINT of the segment, and the midpoint is the listed option. Midpoint outcome, not distance.

Decided by comparing lengths AP and AB through the distance formula, so LO-1 rather than the section formula. The stem is faulty: P(2,1) lies on the LINE through A(4,2) and B(8,4) but outside the segment, so the premise that it lies on segment AB is false even though AP = AB/2 holds numerically.
Midpoint of QR compared with a parametrised point to solve for a. Ratio 1:1, so the midpoint outcome.
Solved by PA squared = PB squared for a point on the y-axis - equidistance via the distance formula. The midpoint of AB is never computed, so LO-3 does not apply despite the word bisector.
Assertion-reason on the distance formula itself: the reason quotes it correctly, the assertion's value of y fails the computation. Tests the distance outcome directly.
Equidistant point on the x-axis, found from PA squared = PB squared. Distance outcome; the midpoint coincidence is incidental to both points lying on the axis.
Equidistant point on the y-axis from two OFF-axis points, so the distance equation must genuinely be expanded and solved. No midpoint shortcut exists here.
Distance formula with trigonometric coordinates; the identity sin squared plus cos squared equals 1 finishes it. Pure distance.
Reflection in the x-axis - a sign rule on the ordinate. No distance, section, midpoint or area outcome covers reflections, so only the goal code is legal without distortion.
Uses that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, i.e. equal MIDPOINTS of AC and BD. This is precisely the second half of LO-3, using the midpoint to verify a property of a quadrilateral.
Section formula with the ratio 3:1 given, solved for an endpoint's ordinate.
Pure axis convention: abscissa 0 on the y-axis, negative ordinate below the x-axis. No formula, and no outcome in this frame covers plotting or axis conventions.
Distance of a point from the origin.
The RATIO in which the x-axis cuts a segment, found by setting it k:1 and forcing the ordinate to zero. LO-2.
Distance of a point from the x-axis; the answer alongside the y-axis distance is what separates abscissa from ordinate.
Midpoint of QR matched to a parametrised point to solve for m.
Midpoint formula solved backwards for the unknown endpoint A.
